This week Citi changed its online terms. If you let an AI agent into your account, you are responsible for what it does. That includes whatever a hacker does if the agent leaks your password.

PNC changed its terms the same day. Citizens emailed customers with the same warning. TechCrunch reports JPMorgan and Bank of America made similar moves last month.

Read that as an engineer. The bank is not asking whether the agent made a mistake or got hacked. It is saying: you handed over the key, so every use of that key is yours.

That is a very old rule. We just forgot it applies to agents.

Inside a company there is no contract that settles it, so the question usually gets answered after something breaks, and then it turns into an argument about whose problem it is.

Three questions I would want answered before an agent touches anything that matters:

1. Which named person owns what this agent does with its access?
2. What is the worst single thing it could do, and can that be undone?
3. Can its access be switched off in minutes, without asking anyone?

If the answer to the second one is "no, it can't be undone", the agent should be suggesting the action and a human should be doing it.

Would you give an agent the login to your own bank account today?

🎯 11/20 News: Markets priced Anthropic above $2T at its peak, but the rest of the stack is busy capping agent risk. Banks are dumping liability on customers. Salesforce is rationing tokens.

💰 Anthropic priced at $83, opened at $111.50, peaked at $114.99 (above $2T), and closed at $97.17, up 17%. The $81.3B raise is the largest IPO ever. Only the seven co-founders sold. Wall Street still slid. Turns out a record debut doesn't revive the AI trade.

This week, AI got three new price tags: one for its shares, one for its tokens, and one for its mistakes.

1) The share price. Per Anthropic, its IPO priced at $83 a share, above the $70–$78 range, with 980 million shares sold. Per Reuters, the stock first traded at $111.50 on Thursday, about 34% higher, in what it called the largest IPO in US history.

2) The token price. Per Google, Gemini 4 Neon launched at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Google says it ranks #3 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

3) The liability price. Per TechCrunch, Citi, PNC and Citizens have updated their customer terms: if you give a third-party AI agent access to your account, you're responsible for what it does, even if the tool is hacked. Citi's own agents are exempt. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies last month.

Why it matters: the cost of AI is no longer just a subscription line. It's capital, usage and risk, and that last one is landing on the user.

My practical takeaway: before connecting any AI tool to a bank or payment account, read your bank's terms first, and default to read-only access.

Which of these three price tags would you watch most closely?

AfroTech 2026 was my first time on a career-fair floor this size, and I'm walking away with better feedback than I could have planned for. Had to take a week or two to process it all but here we are.
Over four days in Houston I talked with recruiters from Goldman Sachs, Capital One, Morgan Stanley, JPMorganChase, Bank of America, Fidelity, Vanguard, PwC, Intuit, NVIDIA, Dell and more. Lead with what you bring, not what you want. A Capital One recruiter told me my pitch was all about how I'd benefit. I rewrote it that night, came back the next day, and she walked me through it again. Making sure to keep it brief and get to the substance. And from there we really got to further connect. I've seen what not understanding money costs people. That's why I study economics, why I'm on the CFA track, and why I'm building an AI platform to make investing understandable for people who never had a finance class.
That week I brought that story to AfroTech 2026 in Houston.
Things Im now sharpening into my approach
• Tell them what you bring to the table, and keep it short.
• Show that you're actively working on yourself.
• Know exactly what a firm does before you hand them a resume.
I went back to one recruiter the next day with a rewritten pitch. Same person, better conversation.
Grateful to AfroTech for the room, and to everyone who took the time to coach a sophomore with a lot to prove. Back to building.

Thank you to every recruiter who gave me honest feedback. I took notes on all of it.
#AfroTech #AfroTech2026 #Finance #Houston
